title: the third pillar
hook: the third pillar — remember the name, on the breath
carry: earn it clean, share it first, keep the name

segments.voice: Yesterday: vand chakna. Your line was share it first. Today, the third pillar, the one that holds the other two up. Day fourteen.

A stool with two legs holds someone for a moment, if they're careful. Add a third leg, and it holds all day. Honest work, sharing what you earn: both solid. But a person could do both and still run on empty: busy, generous, and forgetting what any of it is for. In the Sikh telling, there's a third leg.
screen: `A STOOL WITH TWO LEGS.` → `BUSY, GENEROUS, AND EMPTY.` → `THE THIRD LEG.`

segments.voice: Naam japna. Naam, the name from day ten: not just a label, but the whole presence of God. Japna means to repeat, to keep saying. So: keep the name. Remember God, again and again, all through the day. Its everyday form has its own word: simran, remembrance. How do you remember something all day long? You tie it to something you do all day anyway. You breathe. Wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath: the word from day one. Some Sikhs do it sitting still before dawn, some with prayer beads, some while they drive or cook. If you've ever wondered whether simply repeating Waheguru counts, it's one of the most common ways Sikhs practice. It can be silent, or a whole room singing the scripture to drums and harmonium. Here's why it sits beside work and sharing. Without it, honest work can turn into pride: look how hard I work. Sharing can turn into a show: look how much I give. Remembering keeps both humble, because it reminds you where the strength to work, and everything you share, came from. And remembering without working or sharing would float off into the clouds. Earn it clean, share it first, keep the name. Three legs.
screen: `NAAM — THE NAME. JAPNA — TO REPEAT.` · `SIMRAN — WAHE IN, GURU OUT.` · `IT KEEPS WORK AND GIVING HUMBLE.` · `WORK, SHARE, REMEMBER, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Feel what you're sitting on, and how it holds you up without your thinking about it. Breathe slowly. If you'd like, let the name ride on the breath: Wahe in, guru out. If that word isn't yours, let each breath carry one thing you want to remember is real. Keep coming back to it.

Naam japna. Keeping the name: remembering God through the day, often on the breath, as simran. The third pillar. Fourteenth word. Seva, Ik Onkar, the root verse twice, kirat karni, vand chakna, naam japna: that's week two.
Your line: earn it clean, share it first, keep the name. That's the whole stool. Next week: the company, the door, the spirit and the book. Day fourteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs practice naam japna by repeating Waheguru in simran, often on the breath or with prayer beads, by reciting daily prayers and by singing the scripture together in kirtan; with honest work and sharing it forms the three pillars of Sikh life.

wahe on the way in, guru on the way out.

fork.setup: you work honestly and share generously, but you feel hollow and proud at the same time. what's missing?
fork.reveal: the third pillar, naam japna, keeps the other two humble. three legs, and the stool stands.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: naam (the name) + japna (to repeat, recite).

trapdoor: what you thought: saying God's name a lot.
what it means: keeping the name: remembering God through the day, the pillar that holds work and sharing together.

what a scholar hears: japna is related to jap, repetition, the same root as the title Japji. simran is related to the Sanskrit smarana, remembering, and naam in Sikh usage is the divine presence itself, not only a word.

notes: The relationship between naam japna and simran is described as simran being naam japna's 'everyday form'; some teachers distinguish them. Confirm.
Breath practice (Wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath) is a common teaching; some teach other patterns. Confirm.
Trapdoor links japna to jap and the title Japji (taught on day 21), and simran to Sanskrit smarana; confirm.
The stool image is the script's own illustration, not a traditional one.

Simran beginners (2026-10-06, Reddit research: beginners ask whether simply repeating Waheguru is 'alright'): the teach says it's 'one of the most common ways Sikhs practice', a description rather than a ruling. Confirm.
